calls.call_name: Introductory Connect: 10-minute chat to gauge interest and schedule discovery.
calls.transcript:
Sales Rep (Sarah): Hi, is this Mike?

Prospect (Mike): Yeah, this is Mike. Who's this?

Sales Rep (Sarah): Hi Mike, this is Sarah calling from ApexLogistics AI. I know I’m catching you out of the blue here. I sent you a note earlier this week about... well, honestly, about the headache of fuel surcharges right now. Do you have thirty seconds so I can explain why I called, and then you can tell me if it’s worth chatting further?

Prospect (Mike): Uh, look, Sarah. I saw the emails. Honestly, I'm stepping into a meeting in ten minutes. We're swamped trying to re-route our Southeast fleet.

Sales Rep (Sarah): That actually sounds exactly like why I'm calling. Most of the logistics directors I speak with are drowning in manual re-routing right now, which is just blowing up their fuel spend. Is that Southeast fleet issue related to inconsistent delivery windows or just pure volume?

Prospect (Mike): It's... well, it's both. Mostly the delivery windows. Drivers are idling waiting for slots, or missing them entirely, and we're burning diesel for nothing. So, yeah, the pain is real. But look, we aren't looking for a new platform.

Sales Rep (Sarah): Totally understand. You probably have a system in place. Is it that you're happy with the current efficiency, or is it just the hassle of switching?

Prospect (Mike): It's the tech stack. We run a legacy ERP. It's... it's old, okay? Custom built on-prem stuff. Every time a vendor says they have an API, it turns into a six-month nightmare for my IT guys. And frankly, upper management is paranoid about cloud security. We handle some sensitive government contracts.

Sales Rep (Sarah): That makes a lot of sense. If I were you, I'd be skeptical too. Here’s the thing—Apex was actually designed to wrap around legacy structures rather than replace them. We don't need to rip and replace. Regarding the security—we’re SOC 2 Type II compliant and work with defense contractors already. If I could show you how we integrate without breaking your current ERP, would you be open to a wider conversation?

Prospect (Mike): Defense contractors? Really?

Sales Rep (Sarah): Yes. We take data custody very seriously.

Prospect (Mike): Hmm. Okay. Look, I can't promise anything. But if you can prove the security side to my CISO, I'm interested in the fuel savings. We're over budget by 15% this quarter just on gas.

Sales Rep (Sarah): That is huge leverage for us to fix. Let's do this—let's set up a Discovery call. I'll bring my Sales Engineer to discuss the ERP hookup, and we can send over our security pack beforehand. How does next Tuesday at 2 PM look?

Prospect (Mike): Uh, let me check... Yeah, Tuesday afternoon works. Send the invite. Include the security documentation, or my CISO won't even let you in the Zoom room.

Sales Rep (Sarah): Will do, Mike. Thanks for the time.

Prospect (Mike): Yep, talk then.
calls.summary: Connected with Mike (prospect) who initially attempted to brush off the call due to time constraints. Successfully hooked him by referencing his current struggle with the Southeast fleet re-routing. Validated that fuel costs and inconsistent delivery windows are major pain points. Uncovered significant technical objections: the firm uses a custom on-prem legacy ERP and has strict data security requirements due to government contracts. Overcame the objection by referencing SOC 2 compliance and experience with defense contractors. Mike agreed to a Discovery call next Tuesday, specifically requesting security documentation for his CISO.

calls.call_name: Discovery Call: 30 minutes uncovering pain points regarding fuel costs and delivery delays.
calls.transcript:
Sales Rep (Alex): Hey Mike, thanks for joining me. Can you hear me alright?

Prospect (Mike): Yeah, Alex, loud and clear. Just a heads up, I’ve got a hard stop at the bottom of the hour. Things are... well, things are a bit chaotic at the Atlanta hub today.

Sales Rep (Alex): Understood, Mike. I appreciate the time given the chaos. I want to make this count. I sent over that agenda yesterday—essentially looking to dig a bit deeper into the fuel cost issues you mentioned on our brief call last week and see if our predictive engine can actually plug into that legacy setup you have. Does that still sound right?

Prospect (Mike): Yeah, that’s the ticket. Look, to cut to the chase... we are bleeding cash on diesel. I pulled the numbers yesterday for the Southeast region, and we’re up about 15% year-over-year on fuel spend, and volume is only up 3%. So, the math isn’t mathing, you know?

Sales Rep (Alex): That is a significant gap. Is that mostly due to idling, or are the routes themselves inefficient?

Prospect (Mike): It’s the routing. We’re reactive. Driver hits traffic on I-85, misses a window, tries to reroute manually, ends up driving an extra 40 miles. It’s a mess. And because of that, our on-time delivery stats for the big retail contracts have dropped below 92%. If we hit 90%, we start paying penalties.

Sales Rep (Alex): Yikes. Okay, so we need to stop the bleeding on fuel and protect those SLAs before penalties kick in. Regarding the tech side—you mentioned last time you’re running a custom on-prem ERP?

Prospect (Mike): Right. It’s... uh... it’s a dinosaur. It’s a custom Oracle build from back in 2010. It’s sturdy, but it doesn’t talk to anything. My biggest worry is that your fancy AI platform is going to require a six-month integration project. We don’t have the bandwidth for that.

Sales Rep (Alex): Totally valid concern. We actually see that a lot with logistics firms of your size. We usually handle that via a secure API gateway that sits on top of the Oracle database, so we don’t have to rip and replace. But, obviously, security is paramount there.

Prospect (Mike): Exactly. And that’s the other hurdle. Sarah, our CISO... she’s tough. We have some government defense sub-contracts. She won’t let anything touch our data unless it’s Fort Knox. I saw you sent the SOC 2 docs, but she’s going to want a full architecture review.

Sales Rep (Alex): We welcome that. We work with federal contractors already. I can bring our Lead Engineer onto the next call to walk Sarah through our encryption and data residency protocols. 

Prospect (Mike): That would be necessary. If Sarah says no, the deal is dead. But if you can convince her... look, we have budget approved for "Digital Modernization" this fiscal year. We need this live before the Q3 peak season hits in August.

Sales Rep (Alex): Got it. So, Q3 is the go-live target. Okay, let’s do this: I’ll propose a time for a Technical Deep Dive early next week. I’ll send over our API documentation and a specific security pack for Sarah beforehand. 

Prospect (Mike): Sounds good. Send it over. I gotta run to put out this fire in Atlanta. Talk soon.

Sales Rep (Alex): Thanks, Mike. Good luck.

calls.call_name: Product Demo: 45-minute walkthrough of the dashboard and routing engine.
calls.transcript:
Sales Rep (Alex): Hey Mike, thanks for jumping on. Good to see you again. And I see we have Sarah joining us as well? 

Mike (Prospect): Yeah, hi Alex. Sarah is our CISO. Like I mentioned, if the security piece doesn’t fly, the fuel savings don't matter. So, uh, she’s here to grill you a bit.

Sarah (Prospect): Hi Alex. Nice to meet you. I won't interrupt the flow too much, but I do have some hard questions about data residency and your API handshakes once we get to the architecture part. 

Sales Rep (Alex): Absolutely, Sarah. Nice to meet you. We actually specialize in working with defense contractors, so I think you'll find our SOC 2 Type II report pretty comprehensive. But let's dive in. I want to respect the 45 minutes. Mike, per our last chat, the goal today is to show you exactly how the 'Route-Optimizer' engine handles that Southeast region chaos you're seeing. 

Mike (Prospect): Exactly. If you can show me how to fix the I-95 corridor delays, I'm listening.

Sales Rep (Alex): Sharing my screen now. Can everyone see the dashboard? Okay, great. So, what you're looking at here represents a live ingestion of fleet data. Imagine this is your Southeast fleet. Right now, your dispatchers are manually adjusting for traffic, right? 

Mike (Prospect): Yeah, it’s mostly Excel and gut feeling. Takes them about three hours every morning.

Sales Rep (Alex): Right. So, look at this module here. Our AI ingests historical traffic patterns and real-time weather. See this simulation? It just re-routed Truck 402 around a predicted bottleneck near Atlanta before the traffic even built up. That saved 14 miles and about 45 minutes. 

Mike (Prospect): Okay, that’s... that’s actually impressive. Does it account for driver mandatory rest breaks? 

Sales Rep (Alex): It does. It automatically factors in DOT compliance. Now, here is the big question you had about the Oracle integration. We don't need to rip and replace your ERP. We use a secure API gateway to pull order manifest data out of Oracle, run the optimization here, and push the route manifest back as a flat file or JSON, whichever your IT team prefers. 

Sarah (Prospect): Hold on. You're pulling data out. Is that data encrypted in transit? And where is it stored at rest? We handle some sub-contracted military logistics, so we can't have data sitting on a public cloud server in a non-compliant region.

Sales Rep (Alex): Great question, Sarah. All data is encrypted via AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.3 in transit. We utilize AWS GovCloud regions for clients with specific residency requirements. We don't co-mingle your data with other tenants.

Sarah (Prospect): Okay. AWS GovCloud is a good start. I’ll need to see your penetration testing results from the last quarter before I sign off on anything. 

Mike (Prospect): Sarah, assuming the docs check out, from an ops perspective, this UI looks like something my team can actually use. It’s not as clunky as the Oracle screens. 

Sales Rep (Alex): Glad to hear that. 

Mike (Prospect): The issue is going to be the budget. We have a hard cap for software initiatives this year. We’re looking at around $130,000 max for the annual license. Where do you guys sit?

Sales Rep (Alex): For the fleet size you have in the Southeast—about 150 trucks—we typically look at around $145,000, but since we want to get this live before your Q3 peak in August, I might be able to structure it with a ramp-up discount. 

Mike (Prospect): If you can get it under $135k, I can sign without going to the Board. 

Sales Rep (Alex): I’ll make a note of that. Let's verify the technical validation first. 

Sarah (Prospect): Agreed. Send me the architecture diagrams and the SOC 2 report. I'll need a week to review.

Sales Rep (Alex): Will do, Sarah. Sending that immediately after this call. Mike, does this timeline still work for a potential August 1st go-live? 

Mike (Prospect): It’s tight, but yes. Let's aim for a decision by March 10th.

Sales Rep (Alex): Perfect. Thanks everyone.

calls.call_name: Technical Deep Dive: 40 minutes addressing API documentation and legacy integration
calls.transcript:
Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): Alright, looks like we have everyone. Mike, thanks for setting this up. And Sarah, I appreciate you making the time. I know security reviews are... well, they're never the highlight of the week.

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): [Laughs dryly] You could say that, Alex. Look, let's just get straight to it. Mike really wants this dashboard, but I’m looking at your API docs and I’m seeing a modern RESTful architecture. That’s great for you, but we are running a custom Oracle E-Business Suite, version 12.1. It’s from 2010. It’s on-prem, behind a strict firewall because of the defense sub-contracts. We can't just open a port for your cloud to talk to our server. That’s a non-starter.

Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): I completely understand, Sarah. And honestly, 90% of our logistics clients are in the same boat—legacy on-prem systems are the standard, not the exception. We don't need you to open inbound ports. 

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): Okay... so how are you pulling the fleet data then?

Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): We use a lightweight, outbound-only agent—the Apex Secure Bridge. It sits on a utility server within your DMZ. It polls your Oracle database via JDBC, encrypts the payload with AES-256 locally, and then pushes it out to our AWS GovCloud instance via port 443. It’s strictly one-way traffic initiated from your side.

Speaker Mike (GlobalFreight): Sarah, that sounds like what we did for the payroll integration last year, right?

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): Mm, similar. Alex, does this agent require root access? Because that would be a hurdle.

Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): No, absolutely not. User-level permissions only, read-only access to the specific shipping tables. We don't touch the financial ledgers. I can send you the specific schema requirements right after this call.

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): Okay, read-only user level is... manageable. What about the return trip? The dashboard is supposed to push optimized routes back to the drivers, right? Does that go back into Oracle?

Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): Great question. Usually, no. To keep the integration simple and secure, we push the optimized routes directly to the drivers' handheld tablets via our mobile API, bypassing the legacy ERP for the write-back. We just send a flat-file summary back to Oracle once a day for reconciliation, which the agent handles on a scheduled batch job.

Speaker Mike (GlobalFreight): That actually helps. We don't want to mess with the core logic in Oracle if we don't have to.

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): Agile... okay. Um, let's talk compliance. You mentioned GovCloud. Are you FedRAMP authorized?

Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): We are FedRAMP Ready and currently in process for Moderate authorization. However, we are fully SOC 2 Type II compliant, and our GovCloud instance is isolated. All data at rest is encrypted, and we have a dedicated tenant for clients with defense exposure.

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): Alright. I’m going to need to see that SOC 2 report and your latest penetration test summary. If those look clean, and assuming the agent really doesn't need root access... I think we can make this work technically.

Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): I have those ready to go. I’ll email them over under our mutual NDA immediately after we hang up.

Speaker Mike (GlobalFreight): That’s great news. Sarah, if you give the green light by Friday, can we stay on track for the Q3 launch?

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): If the pen test is clean, yes. I’ll need about 48 hours to review the docs.

Speaker Alex (ApexLogistics): Perfect. I’ll send the docs now. Mike, I'll hold off on sending the final order form until Sarah gives the thumbs up, but we are looking good for that August go-live.

Speaker Mike (GlobalFreight): Sounds like a plan. Thanks, Alex.

Speaker Sarah (GlobalFreight): Thanks, bye.
calls.summary: Technical deep dive focused on overcoming the integration gap between Apex's cloud platform and GlobalFreight's legacy on-prem Oracle ERP. Sarah (CISO) initially pushed back on firewall adjustments. Alex resolved this by proposing the 'Apex Secure Bridge' (outbound-only agent, read-only access), which satisfied Sarah's security constraints. The team agreed to bypass writing route data back into Oracle to minimize risk, pushing it to driver tablets instead. Sarah requested SOC 2 and Pen Test reports for final sign-off. Timeline for Q3 launch remains viable pending this review.

calls.call_name: Security Review Call: 30 minutes with buyer's InfoSec team to clear data privacy hurdles.
calls.transcript:
Alex (ApexLogistics): Hi everyone, thanks for jumping on. Mike, good to see you again. And Sarah, thanks for taking the time to review the documentation we sent over earlier this week.

Mike (GlobalFreight): Hey Alex. Yeah, we are running a bit tight on time today—Sarah has a hard stop in 30 minutes—so we really just need to clear these final hurdles so I can get the paperwork started. We really want to hit that Q3 peak window.

Sarah (CISO): Right. Hello, Alex. I did go through the SOC 2 Type II report and the Pen Test results you sent on the 4th. The SOC 2 looks standard, no issues there. However, I have two specific concerns regarding the architecture you proposed for the Secure Bridge agent, specifically regarding our government sub-contracts.

Alex: Understood, Sarah. Let's dive right in. What’s the first concern?

Sarah: It’s data residency. In the Pen Test executive summary, I noticed your testing environment was hosted in AWS US-West. For our defense-related logistics, we strictly require data to never leave the US East availability zones due to latency and specific compliance protocols we have with the DoD. If your production environment mirrors your test environment, that’s a blocker.

Alex: That is a great catch, but let me clarify. The testing environment you saw in the report is just for... well, testing. For our Enterprise clients with defense requirements, specifically like GlobalFreight, we provision instances exclusively on AWS GovCloud in the US-East region. We can actually write that stipulation directly into the DPA (Data Processing Addendum). Would that satisfy the residency requirement?

Sarah: Okay... AWS GovCloud US-East. If you can put that in the DPA, that works. But that leads to my second point: Encryption key management. Since we aren't doing a full on-prem install and are relying on this 'Secure Bridge' to push data to the driver tablets, who holds the keys? If ApexLogistics holds the keys, that's a third-party risk my board won't accept.

Alex: Completely get that. We actually support BYOK—Bring Your Own Key—management. You can generate the keys in your own KMS (Key Management System), and we never have raw access to them. The Secure Bridge agent encrypts the payload locally on your Oracle server before it ever hits our cloud. We just route the encrypted packets. We can't see the payload, only the metadata required for routing.

Sarah: Wait, so the payload is encrypted locally before egress?

Alex: Exactly. AES-256. We are essentially blind to the actual cargo manifest contents until it hits the driver's authenticated tablet.

Sarah: Hmm. Okay. That... actually solves the liability issue for me. 

Mike: Sarah, does that mean we’re good to go? The fuel costs in the Southeast are killing us, I need to get this moving.

Sarah: Look, technically, yes. Alex, I need you to send me an updated DPA with the US-East GovCloud clause and the BYOK specification. If I see those in writing, I’ll sign off on the security review by end of day tomorrow.

Alex: Done. I’ll have legal draft that redline and get it to you within the hour. 

Mike: Perfect. Alex, once Sarah signs off tomorrow, send the final Order Form to me. I’ve got the budget approved for the $135k we discussed, assuming we can still get that signed by Friday?

Alex: Absolutely, Mike. I’ll bundle the updated DPA and the Order Form together. 

Sarah: Alright, thanks Alex. Send that over and I'll review. I have to drop. Bye.

Alex: Thanks Sarah, thanks Mike. Talk soon.
calls.summary: Security review call focused on clearing final blockers from the CISO (Sarah). Sarah raised two main objections based on the previously sent documentation: Data Residency (Government contracts require US-East) and Encryption Key Management. Alex clarified that production environments for defense clients are hosted on AWS GovCloud US-East and confirmed the platform supports BYOK (Bring Your Own Key), ensuring data is encrypted before leaving the client's premise. Sarah verbally approved the solution pending an updated DPA. Mike confirmed budget approval at $135k and requested the Order Form for signature by Friday to meet the Q3 launch timeline.

crm_fields.value: Verbal Approval Granted (Pending DPA update)
AWS GovCloud US-East (Defense contract compliance)
BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) with local encryption via Secure Bridge
DPA must specify US-East residency and BYOK specs

Send updated DPA to Sarah; Send Order Form to Mike.

calls.call_name: Proposal Presentation: 25 minutes outlining tiers and implementation fees.
calls.transcript:
Alex (Sales Rep): Hey Mike, thanks for jumping on. Can you hear me alright? 

Mike (Prospect): Yeah, Alex. Loud and clear. Just getting my coffee settled here. 

Alex: No worries. I, uh, appreciate you carving out the time. I know Fridays can be a bit hectic. How’s everything looking on your end after we sent over the security docs for Sarah? 

Mike: Honestly? Silence is golden with Sarah. Since you clarified the Bring Your Own Key setup and the US-East hosting on Monday, she gave the green light. She sent me a note saying the updated DPA looks standard. So, we are... surprisingly, we are technically clear. 

Alex: That is music to my ears. I know that was a hurdle, but I’m glad the Apex Secure Bridge architecture fit the bill. 

Mike: Yeah, me too. So, look, let’s get down to brass tacks. I’ve got the Q3 peak season looming. If we don't start implementation by April 1st, I’m not gonna get the ROI I need for this fiscal year. 

Alex: Understood. That aligns perfectly with what I prepared. I’m going to share my screen—let me know when you see the pricing breakdown. 

Mike: Yep, I see it. 

Alex: Okay. So, based on our discovery and the strict security requirements Sarah mandated, specifically the GovCloud hosting and the encryption protocols, we need to look at the Enterprise Tier. 

Mike: Enterprise? I thought we were looking at the Pro tier based on the initial website check. 

Alex: I wish we could, but the Pro tier relies on multi-tenant public cloud infrastructure. Because you have those defense sub-contracts and need the isolated environment, Enterprise is the only way to support that compliance. 

Mike: Okay... what’s the damage? 

Alex: So, list price for Enterprise, covering your Southeast fleet volume, is $145,000 annually. Plus, there is usually a one-time implementation fee of $12,500 for the custom ERP integration work. Bringing the total to $157,500 for year one. 

Mike: Whoa, whoa. Alex, stop. We talked about this. My signing authority caps hard at $135k. If I have to go to the CFO for a penny more, this gets pushed to Q4, and we miss the launch window. 

Alex: I hear you, Mike. I remember the $135k cap. 

Mike: I can’t do $157k. The product is great, the route optimization in Atlanta was fantastic, but the budget is the budget. 

Alex: Okay. Let me see what I can do here. I want to get this live for you by August just as much as you do. If we can commit to signing the Order Form by end of day today or Monday morning... I can probably classify the integration as part of our 'Strategic Partnership' program. 

Mike: Which means? 

Alex: It means I can waive the $12,500 implementation fee entirely. That brings us down to $145k. 

Mike: Still $10k over, Alex. 

Alex: Right... okay. Look, since we are wrapping up our quarter, I can apply a one-time discount to the platform fee to bridge that gap. If I flat-rate the Year 1 cost at $135,000 even—covering the license, the GovCloud hosting, and the implementation support—can we get signatures today? 

Mike: $135k flat? 

Alex: $135k flat. No hidden fees. 

Mike: And that includes the support for the Oracle integration? We don't want to be left hanging trying to configure that outbound agent. 

Alex: 100%. That includes our "White Glove" onboarding package. We’ll have a dedicated solution engineer assigned to your account for the first 60 days. 

Mike: Alright. You got a deal. 

Alex: Fantastic. I appreciate you working with me on this, Mike. 

Mike: Send the updated Docusign. I’ll get it signed before I leave the office today. 

Alex: Sending it now. It should hit your inbox in two minutes. Let’s get that Southeast fleet optimized. Have a great weekend, Mike. 

Mike: You too, Alex. Thanks.
calls.summary: Alex presented the final proposal to Mike. The conversation focused on reconciling the necessary 'Enterprise Tier' features (required for the security compliance approved by the CISO) with Mike's hard budget cap of $135k. The initial quote was $157,500 ($145k ARR + $12.5k implementation). Mike pushed back firmly on price, threatening a delay to Q4 if it exceeded his signing authority. Alex successfully negotiated a close by waiving the implementation fee and discounting the ARR to meet the $135k flat total, contingent on a signature by Monday. Mike agreed to the terms and committed to signing the Docusign immediately to ensure an April 1st implementation start date.

Waived Implementation Fee ($12,500) + $10k ARR Discount

calls.call_name: Negotiation Call: 20 minutes agreeing to waive 50% of implementation fees for a 2-year commit.
calls.transcript:
Alex (Sales Rep): Hey Mike, thanks for hopping on the line so quickly. I know you're swamped with the Southeast re-routing prep.

Mike (Prospect): Yeah, no worries, Alex. Honestly, I just need to know if we're good to go. I've got the pen ready, but if that order form isn't at one-thirty-five flat, I can't sign it. My hands are tied by the CFO.

Alex: I hear you loud and clear. That's actually... well, that's exactly why I called. I just got off the phone with my Deal Desk and VP regarding that discount request I sent over yesterday.

Mike: Okay... and? Don't tell me they said no.

Alex: Well, it's a yes and a no. Here's the situation: Because we're in Q1, Finance kicked back the request to waive 100% of the implementation fees on a standard 12-month term. They just wouldn't bite on absorbing that cost entirely without a longer commitment.

Mike: Ugh. Alex, come on. We went through the security ringer with Sarah, we did the deep dive... I can't go back to finance and ask for more money. If it's over $135k, we have to push to Q4. I'm serious.

Alex: I know, and I'm not asking you to ask for more money. I advocated for you pretty hard. I told them Q3 go-live is non-negotiable for you guys. So, we structured a workaround that hits your number.

Mike: Okay, I'm listening. How does that work?

Alex: If GlobalFreight can commit to a 2-year agreement instead of the standard one year, my VP authorized me to waive 50% of the implementation fee—dropping it to $6,250. Then, to solve for the rest, we're going to lower the annual platform license to $128,750. So, your total invoice for Year 1 is exactly $135,000. It stays right at your signing cap.

Mike: Two years... hmm. That's a longer commitment than we usually do for new tech.

Alex: I totally get that. But think about it this way: You've already validated the route optimization in the sandbox, and Sarah has signed off on the security. By doing two years, you're actually locking in that lower ARR of $128k for 2026 as well. You're protecting yourself from the standard 5-7% annual uplift.

Mike: So, Year 2 would just be the $128,750? No implementation fee again?

Alex: Exactly. Year 2 is strictly the software cost. So you're saving money in the long run, and you stay flat at $135k for today's signature.

Mike: And the implementation timeline doesn't change? We still start April 1st?

Alex: 100%. Resources are already allocated pending your signature by end of day.

Mike: Alright. Look, that works. If it keeps me out of the CFO's office and gets the system live before the August peak, I can live with a two-year term. The price lock is actually a decent selling point for me internally.

Alex: Perfect. I'm glad we could make that work. I'm updating the Order Form right now to reflect the 24-month term, the 50% implementation waiver, and the reduced ARR. I'll shoot that over via DocuSign in about five minutes.

Mike: Sounds good, Alex. Send it over. I'll get it signed before lunch.

Alex: Thanks, Mike. We're excited to get this rolling. Talk soon.
calls.summary: Alex called Mike to address the rejection of the full implementation fee waiver by the Finance team. Alex (Sales Rep): Yeah, so, on the data breach indemnification, we are totally fine with what Sarah requested. We’re keeping that uncapped for direct damages related to security failures. That’s standard for us given the SOC 2 status. The specific point was Section 8.2, the General Liability Cap. Your team requested a cap of 3x the total contract value. 

Mike (Prospect): Right. That’s standard GlobalFreight policy for vendors handling operational data. 

Alex (Sales Rep): I get that. Since we structured this as a 24-month deal to hit your $135k annual budget cap, a 3x multiplier on the total contract value pushes the liability exposure pretty high for us relative to the SaaS fees. What our legal team proposed—and I think this usually works for your compliance guys—is setting the cap at 2x the fees paid in the preceding 12 months, but keeping the data breach indemnity uncapped. Does that sound reasonable? 

Mike (Prospect): Hmm. So general liability is 2x annual, but data breach is unlimited? 

Alex (Sales Rep): Exactly. So if there’s a standard service failure, it’s capped at double the annual fee. If we lose your data, we’re on the hook fully. 

Mike (Prospect): Okay... yeah, honestly, Sarah’s main concern was the data. I think if you keep the breach language as-is, I can sell the 2x annual cap to Legal. I’ll just tell them it’s the concession we made to get the price lock for Year 2. 

Alex (Sales Rep): Perfect, I appreciate you going to bat for us there. The second point was the 'Force Majeure' clause. Your team added 'pandemic and global supply chain disruption' as specific triggers. We’re fine with that, obviously, given the industry you’re in.

Alex (Sales Rep): Totally understood. We accepted that redline as written. The last item was just the payment terms. I noticed the redline changed it from Net 30 to Net 45.

Alex (Sales Rep): It's not a dealbreaker, but since we waived 50% of the implementation fee to get down to that $128k ARR, my VP usually insists on Net 30. However... look, if you can commit to signing this by close of business today so we can book it for Q1, I’ll just approve the Net 45 on my end and take the heat. 

Mike (Prospect): [Laughs] Okay, deal. If you get me the clean copy within the hour, I’ll sign it before I leave today. 

Alex (Sales Rep): You got it. One last logistical thing—assuming we get the signature today, our Customer Success VP, Jenna, wants to schedule the Kickoff Call. We were aiming for April 1st, which is a Tuesday. Does that still work for you and Sarah? 

Mike (Prospect): Let me check the calendar... uh... April 1st is okay, but Sarah is out that morning. Can we do the afternoon? Maybe 2:00 PM EST? 

Alex (Sales Rep): 2:00 PM EST works. I’ll send the invite pending the signature. We’ll cover the API credential handoff and the training schedule for the Southeast regional managers then. 

Mike (Prospect): Sounds like a plan. Send over the updated Order Form and I’ll get it done. 

Alex (Sales Rep): Will do, Mike. Thanks for the partnership on this. Talk soon. 

Mike (Prospect): Thanks, Alex. Bye.
